stimulus.title: Measuring a platform’s rotational inertia
stimulus.html:
Students want to find the rotational inertia I of a horizontal platform that turns on a vertical axle. A light string is wound on a small spool of radius r = 0.020 m fixed to the axle, runs horizontally over a light, frictionless pulley and holds a hanging mass m. When the mass is released from rest, it falls and the platform spins up. The string does not slip on the spool.

For a hanging mass m falling with acceleration a, the tension in the string is m(g − a), and the spool’s radius links a to the platform’s angular acceleration. The students’ results (use g = 9.8 m/s²):

Hanging mass m (kg)Fall time t (s)Acceleration a (m/s²)m(g − a) (N)
0.0507.260.03040.488
0.1004.760.07060.973
0.1503.870.10681.454
0.2003.280.14871.930
0.2502.960.18262.404

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the students could use to collect the data in the table. Include the measurements they make, the equipment for each, and one way to reduce experimental uncertainty.

rubric.point: Measures the hanging mass with a balance and the fall distance with a meterstick (or uses a motion detector or photogate for the motion)
Measures the fall time from rest with a stopwatch (or photogate) and finds a = 2d/t²; or measures a directly with a motion detector
accept: a = 2d/t² from timing a known distance
motion detector gives a from the slope of v-t

rubric.point: Reduces uncertainty: repeats each trial several times and averages, and/or uses several different hanging masses
accept: three or more trials per mass, averaged

parts.sample: Measure each hanging mass m on a balance. Mark a fall distance d = 0.800 m with a meterstick. Release the mass from rest and time its fall over d with a stopwatch (or a photogate at the bottom). Calculate a = 2d/t², since it starts from rest with constant acceleration. Repeat each mass three to five times and average the times, then repeat for five different hanging masses.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe what quantities the students should plot to obtain a straight line whose slope can be used to find I, and explain how they would find I from the slope.

rubric.point: Plots m(g − a) (the tension) against a (or 1/a against 1/m, or another linear choice with a correct slope)
accept: tension on the vertical axis, a on the horizontal

rubric.point: Relates the slope to I correctly: slope = I/r², so I = (slope)r² (for 1/a vs 1/m, slope = I/(gr²))

parts.sample: For the platform, the string’s torque gives F_T r = Iα, and with a = rα, F_T = (I/r²)a. The tension is m(g − a). So plot m(g − a) on the vertical axis against a on the horizontal axis: a straight line with slope I/r². Then I = (slope) × r². (Any friction torque at the axle adds a constant, which shows up as the intercept, not in the slope.)

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: On the grid provided, plot the data needed to make the graph you described in part (b). Label the axes with quantities and units, use a linear scale, and draw a best-fit line.

rubric.point: Axes labeled with the plotted quantities and units
Linear scales chosen so the data fill most of the grid; all five points plotted correctly
accept: points within about half a grid square

rubric.point: A single straight best-fit line (not connect-the-dots), with points scattered on both sides
accept: one ruler line through the trend

parts.sample: Vertical axis: m(g − a) in N, from 0 to 2.5 N. Horizontal axis: a in m/s², from 0 to 0.20 m/s². The five points (0.030, 0.49; 0.071, 0.97; 0.107, 1.45; 0.149, 1.93; 0.183, 2.40) lie close to a straight line; a ruler line through them crosses the vertical axis a little above zero.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the rotational inertia of the platform, using the slope of your best-fit line.

rubric.point: Finds the slope from two points on the line (not data points unless on the line), with units: about 13 kg (N per m/s²)
I = slope × r² with a correct value and units, about 0.0050 kg·m²
accept: a value consistent with the student’s slope

parts.sample: Two points on the line: (0.040 m/s², 0.60 N) and (0.180 m/s², 2.35 N). Slope = (2.35 − 0.60) N / 0.140 m/s² ≈ 12.5 kg. I = (slope)r² = (12.5 kg)(0.020 m)² = 0.0050 kg·m².
